examples.problem_statement:
Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning.

That people ______ the musical features of birdsongs suggests that despite the vast evolutionary gulf between birds and mammals, songbirds and humans share some common auditory perceptual abilities.

A mimic
B recognize
C relish
D are confounded by
E can make out
F are puzzled by

solution.operation: Read what the sentence claims: some human ability toward the musical features of birdsongs suggests that humans share a perceptual ability with songbirds.
solution.result: The blank must name an ability that humans actually possess, and it must be perceptual.
solution.description: Trace the logic of the sentence first: because the main clause concludes that humans and songbirds share an auditory perceptual ability, whatever fills the blank has to be evidence that humans have that ability.

solution.operation: Test 'are confounded by' (D) and 'are puzzled by' (F) against that requirement.
solution.description: Insert each of these two choices and check them against the requirement from step 1: they describe a failure to perceive, so they do not allow for the existence of the ability the sentence needs, and both drop out.

solution.result: Both make sense in the blank but are eliminated: each designates more than just perception, and neither has a partner among the choices that would produce a similar sentence.
solution.description: Check the remaining tempting choices on two counts at once. They read acceptably, but each carries meaning beyond perception, and Sentence Equivalence needs a matching second word, which neither one has.

solution.result: The two completed sentences are alike in meaning and both express plain perception.
solution.description: Confirm the surviving pair: these two are the only choices that both stay within perception and mean the same thing as each other, satisfying the requirement that the two completed sentences be alike in meaning.

examples.answer: Choice B: recognize; AND Choice E: can make out

key_reminders: The two correct choices must produce completed sentences alike in meaning, not merely two sentences that each make sense.
The word in the blank has to be consistent with the claim the rest of the sentence draws from it.
A choice that designates more than the sentence needs is weaker than one that names exactly the required idea.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'are confounded by' and 'are puzzled by' as a synonym pair, ignoring that they contradict the sentence's conclusion that humans share the perceptual ability.
Selecting 'mimic' or 'relish' because it reads well in the blank, without checking that a second choice creates a sentence similar in meaning.

examples.problem_statement:
Recently, the tuition at most elite private high schools has been rising more quickly than inflation. Even before these increases, many low- and middle-income families were unable to afford the full tuition costs for their children at these schools. With the new tuition increases, these schools will soon be attended solely by students from affluent families.

Which of the following would it be most useful to determine in order to evaluate the argument?

(A) Whether students from affluent families are more likely to prefer public or private high schools
(B) Whether most students from low- and middle-income families are academically qualified to attend elite private high schools
(C) Whether low-income families are less likely to be able to afford tuition costs than middle-income families
(D) Whether graduates of elite private high schools typically earn higher salaries as adults than do people who did not graduate from these schools
(E) Whether grants or scholarships are available for students from economically disadvantaged families

solution.operation: Identify the question type from the words 'evaluate' and 'most useful to determine'.
solution.description: Read the question stem before the argument and classify it: the phrases 'evaluate' and 'useful to determine' mark this as an Evaluate the Argument question, which sets what the right answer must do.

solution.operation: Deconstruct the argument into its parts: tuition rising faster than inflation (fact); many low- and middle-income families already could not afford it (fact); these schools will soon be attended solely by affluent students (prediction).
solution.result: Conclusion: private high schools will have only rich students.
solution.description: Separate facts from conclusion by labeling each sentence. The first two are stated facts, so the third, a prediction about the future, is the conclusion the answer must bear on.

solution.operation: State the goal and surface the assumption: the author assumes there is no way for lower-income students to attend, that is, no loans, no scholarships.
solution.result: The right answer must have two paths, one making the conclusion more likely valid and one making it less likely valid.
solution.description: Before touching the choices, fix the target. Name the gap the conclusion depends on, and note that a correct Evaluate answer must be a question whose two possible answers push the conclusion in opposite directions.

solution.operation: Eliminate (A), (B), (C), and (D) against the two-path test.
solution.result: (A) out: the conclusion is that private schools have only wealthy students, not that all wealthy students attend private schools. (B) out: qualified or not, these students still cannot afford the schools, so the conclusion holds either way. (C) out: the argument combines low- and middle-income families rather than distinguishing them. (D) out: it addresses the consequences of attending, not whether students can afford to attend.
solution.description: Work from wrong to right, checking each of the four choices for whether its two possible outcomes actually move the conclusion in opposite directions. Each of these fails, either by reversing the conclusion's direction, by leaving it equally strong both ways, or by addressing something outside it.

solution.operation: Apply the two-path test to (E): if grants and scholarships exist, lower-income students may afford these schools; if they do not exist, those students cannot attend.
solution.result: (E) can either weaken or strengthen the conclusion, so it is correct.
solution.description: Run both branches of the surviving choice explicitly. One branch hurts the conclusion and the other supports it, which is exactly the behavior an Evaluate answer must show.

key_reminders: An Evaluate answer must have two paths: one answer to it makes the conclusion more likely valid, the other less likely valid.
Sort each sentence into fact or conclusion before evaluating answers; the prediction about the future is the conclusion here.
A choice that leaves the conclusion equally strong whichever way it resolves is wrong.
common_mistakes: Picking (B) because qualification feels relevant, missing that unqualified and unaffordable both lead to the same conclusion.
Picking (C) by splitting low- from middle-income families when the argument treats them as one group.
Reversing the conclusion into 'all wealthy students attend private schools' and so being drawn to (A).

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion via tone and contrast cues

examples.problem_statement:
Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text.

It is a sad but just indictment of some high school history textbooks that they frequently report as (i) ______ claims that historians hotly debate or that are even completely (ii) ______ by (iii) ______ primary sources.

Blank (i): A factual, B controversial, C sensational
Blank (ii): D resolved, E corroborated, F contradicted
Blank (iii): G dubious, H incomplete, I reliable

solution.operation: Read the word 'indictment', meaning a charge of wrongdoing.
solution.result: The sentence sharply criticizes the textbooks, so every blank must support that critique.
solution.description: Start from the tone word that governs the whole sentence. Because 'indictment' signals a charge of wrongdoing, each blank has to be filled with a word that keeps the criticism intact.

solution.operation: For Blank (i), test 'controversial' against the phrase 'claims that historians hotly debate'.
solution.description: Try the choice that merely restates the context. Reporting hotly debated claims as controversial would be neither surprising nor inaccurate, so it produces no criticism and cannot be right.

solution.operation: Weigh 'sensational' against 'factual' for Blank (i), then check against the rest of the sentence, which concerns the textbooks' relationship to primary sources.
solution.result: 'factual' (Choice A) is chosen, since it implies gross inaccuracies and the critique centers on accuracy rather than tone.
solution.description: Compare the two remaining candidates on what kind of fault each alleges. 'Sensational' charges melodramatic tone while 'factual' charges inaccuracy, and the rest of the sentence, about primary sources, shows the critique is about accuracy.

solution.operation: For Blank (ii), use the 'even' preceding it, which demands a word further from factual than 'hotly debated'.
solution.result: 'contradicted' (Choice F) fits; 'resolved' and 'corroborated' are the opposite of what is needed.
solution.description: Let the escalating 'even' set the requirement for this blank: it needs something stronger against factuality than mere debate. Only 'contradicted' escalates that way, while the other two point the opposite direction.

solution.operation: For Blank (iii), determine what the primary sources must be, given that the accuracy critique rests on the textbooks' divergence from them.
solution.result: The sources must be authoritative, so 'reliable' (Choice I) fits; 'dubious' and 'incomplete' suggest the opposite.
solution.description: Ask what quality the sources need for the criticism to land. Since the textbooks are faulted for diverging from these sources, the sources must be authoritative, which 'reliable' supplies and the other two undercut.

examples.answer: Choice A: factual; Choice F: contradicted; Choice I: reliable

key_reminders: 'Indictment' marks the sentence as criticism, so every blank must sustain the critique.
'even' before a blank signals escalation: the word must go further than the idea just stated.
The primary sources must be authoritative for a divergence from them to count as an error.
common_mistakes: Filling Blank (i) with 'controversial' because it echoes 'hotly debate', producing an accurate report rather than an indictment.
Choosing 'sensational' for Blank (i), shifting the charge to tone when the rest of the sentence makes it about accuracy.
Putting 'corroborated' or 'resolved' in Blank (ii), which reverses the escalation that 'even' demands.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion via paragraph theme

examples.problem_statement:
Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text.

Richard M. Russell said 52 percent of the nation's growth since the Second World War had (i) ______ invention. He said, (ii) ______ research, the government's greatest role in assuring continuing innovation is promoting a strong, modern patent office. "Unless we can (iii) ______ original ideas, we will not have invention," Mr. Russell said. Speculating on the state of innovation over the next century, several inventors agreed that the future lay in giving children the tools to think creatively and the motivation to invent.

Blank (i): A been at the expense of, B no bearing on, C come through
Blank (ii): D in addition to restricting, E aside from supporting, F far from
Blank (iii): G evaluate, H protect, I disseminate

solution.operation: Take a quick overview of the paragraph to fix its topic.
solution.result: The topic is the encouragement of invention and innovation.
solution.description: Read the whole paragraph before filling anything in, so that a single controlling theme, here the encouragement of invention and innovation, can govern all three choices.

solution.operation: For Blank (i), apply that theme to the claim about 52 percent of the nation's growth.
solution.result: 'come through' (Choice C) is chosen because it emphasizes the importance of invention; the other choices suggest invention is irrelevant to growth or harmed by it.
solution.description: Match this blank to the theme from step 1. Only a phrase crediting invention for the growth emphasizes its importance, while the alternatives make invention irrelevant or damaged.

solution.operation: For Blank (ii), check which choice continues the theme of encouraging invention.
solution.result: 'aside from supporting' (Choice E) is the only one that does.
solution.description: Screen this blank's three options by the same encouragement theme rather than by grammar alone, since only one of them keeps the government in a supporting role toward invention.

solution.operation: For Blank (iii), carry over the second sentence's emphasis on a strong patent office into Mr. Russell's quotation, which reaffirms it.
solution.description: Link the quotation back to the sentence before it. Since that sentence stresses the patent office and the quotation restates the same thought, the blank needs the verb that names what a patent office does for original ideas.

examples.answer: Choice C: come through; Choice E: aside from supporting; Choice H: protect

key_reminders: Establish the paragraph's overall theme first; in a multi-blank text all blanks must serve it.
A quotation that reaffirms the preceding sentence must be filled with a word consistent with that sentence.
Reject choices that reverse the passage's stance, such as those making invention irrelevant or restricted.
common_mistakes: Filling Blank (i) with 'been at the expense of' or 'no bearing on', which contradicts the paragraph's praise of invention.
Choosing 'evaluate' or 'disseminate' for Blank (iii) instead of the verb that matches the patent-office emphasis of the preceding sentence.
